title: How To Be Funny And Not Just Stupid
author_evidence: wesdood is presented as a Newgrounds forum user: "Member Level 28 Blank Slate"; he calls this material a folder of "funny topics to use in the future."
doc_text:
Today's topic is "How To Be Funny And Not Just Stupid"

CONTENTS
* 1 Be a Comedian: Advice About Nonsense and Opposites
* 2 When Writing Nonsense, be Consistent
* 3 Spend a Little Bit of Time
* 4 The "@#$%^&*" Rule: Being Crass or Tasteless Doesn't Automatically Make Everything Funny
* 5 Avoid Clichés
* 6 Don't plagiarise
* 7 Meta-Humor isn't always as funny as you think it is
* 8 Use In-Jokes Sparingly
* 9 Use Pictures Wisely
* 10 Bias Is Not a Replacement for Humor
* 11 Outright sarcasm is Not a Replacement for Humor
* 12 In The Style Of...
* 13 Advice

1 - Be a Comedian: Advice About Nonsense and Opposites

The truth is often funnier than flat out nonsense. The funniest pages are those closest to the truth.

Blending fact with fiction, or blurring that line makes for better comedy. Now, mind you, this is not a particularly hilarious line, but you get the idea.

Patent nonsense can be hilarious, it may get a laugh the first time, but it quickly gets dull. If someone types in "Harry Potter", the article should have more to do with Harry Potter than if they typed in "Dinosaur". They want to read a humorous slant on Harry Potter, not an article on a Dutch mink farmer with laser-beam eyes. Nonsense has been done before — over, and over, and over again.

2 - When Writing Nonsense, be Consistent

If you can't stay close to the truth, try to be consistent across many articles. A good example is the Oprah conspiracy series. Despite the fact that it is entirely incoherent, it's incoherent across a large span of history. This is Good.

Random humour can be funny if it is not seen as being serious. Keep in mind that not everyone will get the joke, and often get upset at those who write random humour.

7 - Meta-Humor isn't always as funny as you think it is

Meta-humor is like fine, aged wine, it must not only have be around for a long time, but also has to have intrinsic value in order for it to be any good. Century-old bad wine is one hundred years old, but it's still bad wine.

8 - Use In-Jokes Sparingly

Just 'cause it's funny to you and three of your friends doesn't make it funny to us. Most in-jokes are "had to be there" moments, or rely on several other situations/experiences to understand exactly what makes it funny. They're hard to explain, and fail to be humorous in a stand-alone situation.

9 - Use Pictures Wisely

A picture is a perfect complement to a good joke. But only if it is well made.

10 - Bias Is Not a Replacement for Humor

Never substitute bias in place of humor. While biases and points of view are allowed, often to the extent of encouragement, on Newgrounds, simply writing something like "The Big Mac is a piece of dog shit on two buns" or "OMG DS > PSP LAWLH@X" is not funny by itself. Instead, explain, in lavish detail, what makes these things so great or terrible. Remember, you aren't the only person on this planet. Try to keep your stuff funny, but not insulting. Unless the insulting is humorus on several levels.

11 - Outright sarcasm is Not a Replacement for Humor

Clearly stating what is either right or obvious in a sarcastic manner comes off less as funny, and more as politically resentful or bitter.

12 - In The Style Of...

For some articles, doing the article in the style of what the article is about can be amusing. For example, a topic on Redundancy would be redundant, repetitive, and repeat itself.

13 - Advice

Remember rule one. If something is coherent, and closer to the truth, it is funnier than pure nonsense.

Often, official, professional-sounding prose kicks the humor up a bit. Consider your tone as you write threads. Would an authoritarian, encyclopedic tone make this even better, or would slack-jawed drivel work best as its own sort of irony? Do outbursts work? Try different styles to see if it improves your content.

SeizureDog added: Never say something is going to be funny before you tell your joke. It will either make people have too high of expectations or they will actively try to not like it.

title: What's the key to good comedy writing for animation and comics
author_name: ngman7, MemeBean975, OlTrout, and other Newgrounds BBS participants
author_evidence: The most rubric-like reply is by MemeBean975, shown as "Browse All Posts (7)" and "Member Level 09 Gamer" rather than a comedy professional.
doc_text:
ngman7: Hi. I want to produce my own animation and comics and I'd like to know what's the key to good comedy writing for both animation and comics?

I intend to produce comedic works and I want to produce works for kids and general audiences.

You want humor that stands out and resonates with kids and general audiences.
Part of the reason a show like Animaniacs was successful was that the humor worked on more than one level. This is why the show was popular with both kids and adults.

Something that may seem funny to a creator or whoever is writing animation and comics might not seem funny to other people.

How do you know what's funny and what isn't?

FlameDaddyDoc: My best advice to you would be to watch some cartoons for all ages that you find funny and write down everything you laugh at and then if you notice any similarities between them all write it down. You'll likely find a good way to come up with your own humor after seeing what works for others

OlTrout: In animation, I really love visual humour. Things like wacky movements that wouldn't be possible in real life. It's subtle things that resonate with me like stretchy limbs and gags that involve gravity not catching up to the characters until they realize they're going to fall. I love when characters are surprised and their eyes pop out. I love when characters hover above the ground for dramatic effect.

I think back to cartoons in the 90s where voice actors put on silly voices and weren't simply just the voice of a famous actor. I like dramatic walks. I like when animals 'roll up their sleeves' even though it's just fur. I like gags where animals are wearing underwear under their fur.

I know it's not writing that I'm talking about, but these are what make cartoons extra special for me.

MemeBean975: When making a comedic sketch, you wanna make something that is unpredictable because that's what makes a joke funny. You can start off with an "interesting" sentence such as:

Jack had an apple to eat

and add to that.

most jokes have a topic (your base idea/sentence) misdirection (this is when you confuse the audience and make the hard-hitting part of the joke unpredictable) punchline (this is what makes a joke funny and is the hard-hitting part of the joke)

so now let's go back to our sentence and add what we have learned:

Jack had an apple to eat, (topic) but then a cat walked by (misdirection) and he punched her in the face.

now was this funny? no, that's because it was uninteresting. unpredictability, and the fact whether or not the or not if the punchline is interesting.

if you are trying to make jokes for a broad audience try to make them simple and general, rather than picking a subject such as a video game, pick a general topic that everyone can adhere to such as school life or daily challenges.

- Hope this helped you m8

title: Humor and writing
author_name: Deleted member 56686 and Writing Forums participants
author_evidence: Participant Sonata explicitly says: "I am not a writer - I write what some kind people on WF think is poetry." The site describes itself as a community for "writers and poets of all abilities."
doc_text:
Deleted member 56686: As someone who prides himself on writing comedy, I am fortunate enough to find things to write about in a humorous vein rather easily. To me, I guess it comes naturally. What about you? Do you like to insert humor in your work? Where do you find humor to write about? Do you find it adds or takes away from what you are trying to do?

midnightpoet: I use humor whenever I can, but sometimes it doesn't work. I tried some over the top black humor in my last LM contest story and I don't think it went over well. I know some people say they don't do humor very good. One key is self-deprecation, another exaggeration for effect.

Foxee: The first writing forum I joined (kind of blindly) was a humor-writing forum. That and reading both shaped my writing. Dean Koontz and Terry Pratchett are both fantastic at writing something that's intense and yet turn a phrase or throw in a cockeyed truth a the same time that adds a moment of levity. So unless it's entirely inappropriate for something that I'm writing, I'll usually allow humor to find its way in, even if it's not really a humor piece. In my opinion the truth is what makes something funny, serious, and/or real. Sometimes all at the same time.

Plasticweld: I find it much easier to be funny in person and in real life than in writing. The art of showing the drama, the emphases, in writing is truly an accomplishment. I am a funny guy, sarcasm, twists of my words or just sometimes the right body language I can make just about anything funny. The pauses in writing, the timing often elude me.

Gavrushka: Inappropriate and unexpected humour can often turn a good section into an exceptional one, but forced or 'canned' humour really removes my immersion.

JustRob: I have read books in which writers have included humour without context simply for its own sake and I find it an annoying practice. If we include humour then surely like any other component of our writing it must add to the progress of the story. In particular the manner in which the characters themselves react to the humour is important. After all, if they don't see the humour then why should the writer expect the reader to see it either?

As is often the case I must refer back to that all-important character, our target reader. If we perceive them as having a sense of humour then it is quite valid to stimulate it in our writing and if we have them defined clearly enough in our minds then we will know what kind of humour is likely to succeed.

Sonata: Humour has its place in life, its place in writing - prose, poetry, all sorts really - but for me it has to be natural humour, not forced. Foxee mentioned Dean Koontz, who puts odd bits of humour in without trying to force them to be funny. They just are natural humour in some parts of his books. And as such I found them fitting perfectly in what he was writing.

title: Sketch Comedy
author_evidence: theoroll posts a self-made project with "All feedback is welcome"; machardi calls the framing principle "a lesson I've learned recently, (and am still learning)."
doc_text:
theoroll: I'm using an HVX200 for a sketch comedy project. All feedback is welcome.

machardi: Honest feedback? It's okay, overall, but could be better.

At any given moment you should ask yourself: "What am I filming?"

With the last shot you have two choices of what you could film (well, an infinite #, but here are two)
A. A pier, sitting on the water, with a guy running/dancing along it. OR
B. A guy running/and dancing on a pier.

Do you see what I'm saying? You shot A, which is majestic, instead of B, which would've been funnier. The audience doesn't really get to see what's going on, because fully 90% of the visual information you are giving them is "Here's a pier. Here's a pier. Here's a pier. Here's a pier. Here's a guy. here's a pier." At 24 frames per second. If you're going to buffet my brain with info, shovel "here's a guy running goofily".

Don't mistake this as an argument against wideshots. There's humor in "The vast desert. A guy runs through it." that would be lost in "A guy runs through the desert."

People doing goofy things is only marginally funny. People doing goofy things while other people watch, is considerably funnier. The awkwardness of that guys moves would be a 1000x more appreciated, by the audience, if he were doing it at the mall, or in a gym. What makes being awkward funny is the concept of being watched.

Are you familiar with the concept of a "reveal"? Basically in humor, the idea is the very last thing you say, or see, should undermine and redefine everything that happened before it. That's what makes people laugh. If you show off your punch line early, and then just keep showing them the punch line, it's not new, and doesn't require any active reinterpretation by the audience, thats when jokes get old.

Justyn: I've produced a few sketches and about to do another series so it's about doing what you think is funny and keeping it brief and fast and too the point. You got 10 seconds to hook 'em and it has to sustain and be cut accordingly... brevity and constant enhancment of the concept through the completion of the humor...

machardi: Once you've asserted your premise, there has to be something else, eventually. Satire only works if you take the source material, and really explore the various facets of it. Your source material (Modern Dance) is fairly rich, but you mine a very limited range of it (Self-Important 'profound' self reflective speech, mixed with 'funny' dance moves), you don't add anything or enhance the joke.

If he'd spent the whole video just talking about how he likes hitting cops, it would've gotten old. That's -enhancing- the joke.

title: What are Dad Jokes?
author_evidence: Irishman approaches the board as a learner: "I’m curious about the term, and I’m curious about the type of humor... Please help me understand."
doc_text:
Irishman: I’m curious about the term, and I’m curious about the type of humor.

What makes a joke a "Dad joke"?

Also, that term seems to have a negative tone, a commentary on the quality of the joke.

Please help me understand.

Mangetout: They’re usually the sort of jokes that make people groan rather than laugh. Corny humour. Often based on puns.

Also sometimes they have a disproportionally long setup for a very small and often anticlimactic punchline (similar to shaggy dog stories).

The appeal of them is sort of meta-humour; we’re laughing not because the joke was funny, but because dad did the dad joke again.

running_coach: Basically, the punchline is a bad pun with a labored or contrived setup.

title: What defines a traditional British sitcom?
author_name: jak ohara and British Comedy Guide forum participants
author_evidence: jak ohara says: "I am a Media Studies student" and later "I am studying A-level media."
doc_text:
jak ohara: I am a Media Studies student and I've been given the task to try and define what a traditional British sitcom is.

But I want to understand what it is that makes a sitcom such as Fawlty Towers and Only Fools And Horses so different from Peep Show. Obviously there's the point of view shots and so on but what really defines a traditional sitcom?

Aaron: Traditional sitcom: studio, live audience, gags and setups.

Peep Show: closed set, no audience, humour derived from situations (mostly social faux pas and the like).

jak ohara: Performing in front of a live audience meant actors could play of an audience's response also a live set was what traditionally made the British sitcom so special as it meant people could see how shows where put together and there response to the situation unfolding in front of them was recorded and included in the show that was broadcasted.

Although Peep Show regularly makes witty humorous remarks, gags on programs such as Fawlty towers where more direct to the subject. For example in Fawlty Towers when Basil is attending to German Guests and tries not to mention the war but it seems everything he does results in the war being brought up. In Peep show it's more banter between the two main characters.

Aaron: Instant audience feedback. Gives the performers something to bounce from and a sense of timing. Also an instant guage of if a joke is actually funny or not.

title: Help with stand-up
author_name: Jason Simmons, Park Bench, Cheagle, and British Comedy Guide forum participants
author_evidence: Jason says he has done stand-up only "for a short while now (mainly 5 min spots)"; Cheagle says, "I haven't actually done my first gig yet."
doc_text:
Jason Simmons: I have been doing stand-up for a short while now (mainly 5 min spots) which is built up of one liners and a few stories but, my question is how do I develop my stories so that there are more jokes in them or that they are funnier??

The main problem I face with them is that when I tell a story to a group of friends it may get loads of laughs but, then if I try to 'perform' that story on stage as part of a routine it gets a totally different response (usually silence or a small mumur of laughter).

Park Bench: Ever notice that when a story is told and all those who were there find it funny, yet noone else, prompting the line 'you had to be there' ? Jokes will always be set-up and punch. It may not always be obvious, but that's how they work. When considering your stories, you should be able to find both parts.

I see the next level for you is to start to cluster jokes so you have a few around the same topic. This should allow you to generate a 'joke story' where you can change the delivery, reaction, adjectives and type of speech to make it personal.

One thing is true for everyone. You should get your set memorised so you know it backwards. The intro, the links, the body language and the outro.

Garry Lee: What strikes me is that:

1) I didn't find any of those stories particularly funny
2) It seemed like a long setup for a not-so-great payoff
3) Every last line in your stories there ends with an expletive, like you're using that as a crutch to get a laugh

Also, it might not be best to use your friends for a barometer of what is funny, have you ever thought they might just be humouring you? The people that you don't know have no obligation to laugh, after all.

Cheagle: Basically, I agree with Park Bench in that 'you had to be there' automatically means that something won't be funny to a comedy audience. Chances are, if you're telling a friend about something that happened to you, they may well have been there, thus laughing at their own memories, or they may know the person/people you were with during said anecdote, and can laugh at knowing what a certain person's reaction would be to a certain situation. They certainly know you and your personal traits. You (and I) need to remember that the audience in a comedy club are very unlikely to know the people you were with, and therefore won't have the same reactions as people that do.

You can play to this when telling them anecdotes. I quite often find myself saying to friends of mine something along the lines of "You would of laughed if you were in such a place the other day" followed by the anecdote that is sometimes littered with things like "You can just imagine him saying that" or "you know what she's like", and nine times out of ten they will laugh at the re-telling, whereas a comedy audience is unlikely to because, again, not knowing people you're talking about, they DON'T know what she's like, and they CAN'T imagine him saying that.

title: One liner Comics
author_name: Steve Sunshine and British Comedy Guide forum participants
author_evidence: The criteria come from fans describing their viewing experience; AngieBaby says, "Personally I find it hard to keep up with the scatter gun delivery. I'd prefer to watch Tim Vine on tele than see him live."
doc_text:
Steve Sunshine: Steve Wright & Emo Phillips were two of the best, and in more recent times Tim Vine and Keith Chegwin have blazed a trail for the snappy silly joke.

AngieBaby: I like a lot of 'one liner' acts, but I've noticed that they don't go down too well at live shows. Personally I find it hard to keep up with the scatter gun delivery. I'd prefer to watch Tim Vine on tele than see him live.that way I can pause and rewind.

Matthew Stott: I like one liners, like Tim Vine, but generally prefer a short set from them, if that's all they're going to do. Can feel a bit insubstantial and unsatisfying if it's a full length show.

Ben: The problem is that it's going to be very hard for these one liner comics to break through. Tim Vine is already the master at it, so is anyone taking it in a different direction?

Steve Sunshine: I think Persona & peronality can play a vital role. With Steve Wright & Emo Phillips you buy into their weird worlds immediately. and their timing & delivery are immaculate. Stuart Francis & Tim Vine on the other hand are very affable & likeable. Tim Vine hardly even tries to pretend that he's not telling jokes & has some great self effacing stuff. However when I saw him in a smaller venue years ago the audience stopped laughing after about 5 or 6 jokes and it was all a bit awkward after that. But he's a lot more well known now & audiences know what they're going to get from him.

Matthew Stott: Absolutely; probably why I can't take Jimmy Carr over a longer set, but can for a short set.

title: Sketch Writing
author_name: Lee and British Comedy Guide forum participants
author_evidence: Lee frames himself as a learner: "I get frustrated with myself that I don't have those moments within my own writing" and describes forum sketches as practice and learning.
doc_text:
Lee: I think it's excellent to see people practicing on here. Hopefully learning with every new sketch they write. Feedback is fun and when it works the community is great.

I get the sense it's going nowhere. It's all the same-old same-old.

When was the last time you read a sketch and got genuinely excited?

I get frustrated with myself that I don't have those moments within my own writing. It makes me question and doubt why I am bothering. A part of me just wants to write some funny shit. But there's another part that wants to write something that matters. Not necessarily in a way that makes a change, as a political comedian would. But something with weight. Something probably much deeper than that. It's the scene, joke, comedian you think about when you ask yourself why are you writing. It's not like I'm striving to be considered an inspiration to anyone. It's more about creating that moment when you get excited about writing, where you think "I wanna do that" - "I want to create that moment". Again, it's not about creating a catchphrase or the next Dead Parrot sketch. It's about stirring the emotion that makes writing feel like an art form. Something that resonates deep within the human conscious.

It was more about originality in comedy. And how we can start writing something that we actually care about, rather than just another throw away sketch that we've seen someone else do already.

AJGO: Maybe it takes longer pieces to develop an understanding of characters, style, and rhythm that would engage you beyond the usual.

Lee: There are lots of excellent sketches posted on here. Lots better than what's shown on TV. Some brilliant stuff in fact.

I wanna know what sketch writing means to you. I suppose Steve has kicked off this discussion perfectly. Also, what makes a good sketch? I'm hoping not to mess about with the easy stuff here. I want to dissect it plus think about how it's evolving.

Tim Azure: Sketch writing is just want it says-sketches, thumbnails if you like, we're not all that sure that the characters have lives outside the place and time we see. If you too ambitious, it doesn't work as a sketch.

title: Bill Gravy's Confused Set
author_name: Blenkinsop and British Comedy Guide forum participants
author_evidence: This is a forum workshop: Blenkinsop calls it something he "posted" and revises the amateur character set in response to commenters.
doc_text:
sootyj: Not bad at all, it'll all be in the delivery. A nice snappy collection, of slightly off key, inoffensive, well formed gags.

Blenkinsop: Yeah this would all be the delivery. Bill's not a very good stand-up and an even worse performer. He suffers from poor delivery although these are more like proper jokes than his previous efforts were. It's just he doesen't really know that they are.

roscoff: Like it but doesn't have the same vagueness of the early sketches. I liked the fact that Bill had no idea of basically what he was supposed to do up there so he just talked. This is more sort of gag based. I still like it, but not as much.

Moonstone: I really loved the other Bill Gravy pieces. This one was still good, but he just didn't seem to be the same character.

Blenkinsop: The material is a bit too funny - for Bill. He's lost his way so I need to get him back to being crap

Moonstone: I agree, and for what it's worth I also didn't think it was random enough. A lot of the charm for me came from his randomness, if that's even a word.

Blenkinsop: Yeah think you're right. What I posted was more a straight ahead stand up set

James Williams: It was very different in that every joke was based on the same premise: verbal confusion; mistaking one word for another. I reckon that in the world of stand-up, too, many of them would sail over the audience's head, e.g. the Super Tuesday/Soup(er) Tuesday reference. Not that I didn't find it funny.

title: First attempt at any sort of stand up
author_name: Fatty Otters and British Comedy Guide forum participants
author_evidence: Fatty Otters explicitly labels the material a "first 'attempt' at any sort of 'stand-up' writing" made in a two-hour burst.
doc_text:
Fatty Otters: This was written in a 2 hour burst tonight. Don't expect the best grammar, its more of a stream of conciousness and is my first 'attempt' at any sort of 'stand-up' writing...

FunyHaHA Not Funy Strange: I say record it just because delivery can help with stand up and sometimes its better live than on paper. Your material is to thin and not funny, the comment about your mum could have been if the context and the story was better. never talk about jimll fix it!!!!! the shitting you pants was to obvious and not funny, the whole thing needs rethinking.

Mattytheswan: There were a couple of bits in there I thought were funny. The Mum bit (although a bit obvious) and the "heroine" line. So I reckon if you did that stream of consciousness a few more times you might get 5 minutes out of it.

sootyj: Standup is an organic beast, every gig different for every audience. And writing in every so and um, is fetishising the imperfection.

Tony Cowards, quoted in the thread: The only people who like comedy about comedy are the people doing comedy (and comedy critics).

The only other thing I would say is print that set out then go through it with a highlighter pen marking where you think the audience will laugh. If there are big gaps between the fluorescent marker bits then you need to put more "jokes" in there (and when I say "jokes" I mean things that will make people laugh even if they are not technically jokes e.g. a witty turn of phrase or even a mannerism or "act out").

JaPi: I don't think the final bit about the tower wedding was strong enough, particularly to finish on, but if I were in the audience I'd have been laughing fairly consistently up until then.

Michael Monkhouse: This is classic first-timer in my opinion i.e. there are plenty of ideas but they need focussing. Like the Facebook and 'died doing what he loved' plus the Eiffel Tower, but they need extensive sharpening / punching up. The 'mother' line was bound to get a groan from comedy writers cos it's formula, but could get a huge laugh from punters if it's quicker and less obvious.

NateSean: I just feel like there are certain jokes you should avoid until the audience gets to know you a little better, but that's just me and others might disagree. Even Jimmy Carr didn't start right off with rape jokes.

title: Stand up routine for a gig at Cambrige uni
author_name: andrewlynch88 and British Comedy Guide forum participants
author_evidence: andrewlynch88 says: "This is going to be my first stand up gig" and requests criticism.
doc_text:
andrewlynch88: This is going to be my first stand up gig, some time next week, so let me know what you think of this. Any and all criticism is greatly appreciated. Please be very very harsh on it. Thanks.

Paul W: Good luck, but I think you need to put some serious work in.

I have to agree with James Harris a lot of padding here and no real jokes you seem to have something going but don't give it a punchline.

It needs work but could be pretty funny.

title: Who are the most genuinely talented comedians? - Page 3
author_name: Tommy Griff, Rood Eye, Old Lady Leg, Teddy Paddalack, and other forum participants
author_evidence: The page consists of personal fan judgments; Teddy Paddalack says of performing, "I couldn't do it but I'd love to write for one."
doc_text:
Tommy Griff: I can tell you what makes a poor quality of stand-up, in my view that is. It's comedians who let out a 'ermmmm' post-punchline. In order to signal that they've just made a joke. Absolute 'cringe' as the kids say.

Rood Eye: The fake pause ( "erm . . . ", "and er . . .", etc) is a device intended to pause the dialogue, let the audience catch up and realise that a funny thing has just been said. It also sends a message to the audience that a funny thing is just been said and that a laugh is now expected. Audience members will laugh if the "thing" was genuinely funny but very often they'll also laugh out of politeness even if it wasn't.

Canned laughter, any laughter added during the editing process, or indeed genuine contemporaneous studio laughter serves to tell viewers that lots of people think what has just been said or done was funny. It encourages the viewer to join in with the laughter partly because laughter is infectious and partly because human beings (and many other creatures) like to conform to group norms.

Old Lady Leg: My pet hate is when some comedians just stand there waiting for the laughter to die down after a joke...like they're waiting to gauge how funny the joke was by the time it takes for the chuckles to stop. That's an eternity for me.

Teddy Paddalack: Yes its down to the delivery a lot of comedians never admit it but many are merely 'Actors' reading lines in the desired tempo. But the delivery is a skill in itself as is having the bottle to stand up and do it. I couldn't do it but I'd love to write for one.

Sean Lock isn't bad and Stewart Lee is different , I like any stand ups if they have the material.

title: Fictitious (True Literature Club) | The Art of Critique
author_evidence: The community profile describes The Art of Critique as "A collection of fanart and critiques" and says "If you have a comic or game you want me to check out, requests are always open!"
doc_text:
The writing of the comic is decently good. It manages to strike a balance between the jokes it’s telling and the dialogue being natural. The situations are a little absurd, but the humor doesn’t feel forced, which is a major plus. There’s an element of truth to the jokes as well, so they could be relatable depending on your own experiences. Each strip is four panels long, giving them enough time to establish themselves, set up a joke, and hit a punchline. Even if you don’t start with the first strip of a set, there are enough context clues to give you an idea of what’s happening. In that way, each part is semi-self-contained, which serves the story well.

Characterization is successful, if a bit quirky. The characters seem a bit out there, but it also seems like they have reasons for being the way they are. Horus herself is a great example. She looks and talks very cheerful, but the things she say belie how disenchanted she’s become with life, and you get the impression that she’s holding back a tidal wave of frustration at the cruel hand she’s been dealt. Single, pushing 30, failed to land a job at any of her preferred locations, and just grinning while trying not to let the cracks show too much. She and the others are products of the society they live in, and they’ve all seen enough to expect disappointment more than anything else. In that regard, the comic is rather depressingly "woke," but that’s also a big part of what makes it so funny. If you can’t laugh at what this world throws at you, you may just go insane after all.

So...this comic is generally solid in many regards. The most I could fault it with were a handful of typos. They weren’t on every strip, but I noticed enough of them to say it could be proofread more carefully.

title: If you read through that whole thing, congrats SaveImgflip
author_evidence: The page labels the item "Made by Spy_Crab ... in fun" and presents it as a community-made meme with comments.
doc_text:
